t: Air Fryer Bacon: Times and Temperatures That Actually Work
d: Air fryer bacon times by thickness and doneness, with no-oil layouts, safe handling of hot grease, thick-cut and turkey bacon guidance.
x: Bacon is the food that convinces people to keep an air fryer on the counter: no splatter across the stovetop, and a strip that is crisp at the edges and still chewy in the middle if that is how you like it. It also produces more grease than almost anything else you will cook, and that grease is the whole story. Handle it correctly and bacon is simple. Two warnings before the chart First, times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer and your eyes, not the clock. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food, so a time that works in a 5.8-quart basket can burn bacon in a 2-quart one. Every time below is a range, and the last two minutes are yours to judge. Second, bacon is cured and smoked before it reaches your kitchen, so it is judged by appearance rather than by a target temperature. Turkey bacon is the exception: it is ground poultry, and ground poultry is cooked to 165°F / 74°C like any other ground meat. Bacon type Safe internal temperature Turkey bacon 165°F / 74°C Regular or thick-cut pork bacon Cook until crisp; judge by texture Reheated bacon leftovers 165°F / 74°C No oil, and the layouts that stop sticking Bacon needs no oil at all. t: Air Fryer Baked Potato: Time and Temperature by Size
d: Air fryer baked potato times for russets by size, with the poke-and-oil skin rule, crispy finishes and topping timing that keeps the skin crisp.
x: The air fryer bakes a potato better than a conventional oven in most kitchens: hot air on all sides crisps the skin while the inside turns fluffy, in about half the time and without heating the whole oven. The difference between a great baked potato and a mediocre one is almost entirely preparation — poking, oil and salt — plus the right time for the size. This chart covers russet potatoes by size, the crisp-skin rules and when to add toppings. A potato is one of the safest foods to cook — there is no raw-protein timing to manage — so the whole skill is texture. Times vary by appliance model and potato size. Start checking at the low end and test for tenderness with a fork or skewer — it should slide in with no resistance. Air fryer baked potato chart Poke each potato 6–8 times with a fork, rub the skin with a thin coat of oil and salt it. The pokes let steam escape so the skin crisps instead of splitting, and the oil turns the skin into a shell. t: Air Fryer Chicken Drumsticks: Time and Temperature Chart
d: Air fryer chicken drumsticks time chart for fresh, frozen and breaded legs, with 380°F / 193°C times and the internal temperature rule.
x: Drumsticks are cheap, hard to ruin and crisping in an air fryer they beat almost anything at their price. They are also one of the most undercooked pieces of chicken in home kitchens, because the thick muscle near the bone hides its doneness behind golden skin. This chart gives times for fresh and frozen drumsticks. The skin will look finished before the joint is; the thermometer is the only honest referee, and for all poultry under USDA rules that number is 165°F / 74°C. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, basket size and crowding change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change. Air fryer drumsticks chart: fresh Times assume a preheated basket and a single layer. Drumsticks are irregular, so shaking the basket twice during the cook matters more than with any other cut. The one rule that makes or breaks it is the order: the cutlet cooks fully and crisps FIRST, and the sauce and cheese arrive at the very end. Sauce during cooking steams the breading into sogginess. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage, cutlet thickness and coating change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change. t: Air Fryer Chicken Time and Temperature Chart
d: Air fryer chicken time and temperature chart for breast, thighs, wings, tenders and drumsticks, with the 165°F / 74°C rule and frozen times.
x: Chicken is the food people most want to cook in an air fryer, and the food they most often get wrong. The window between juicy and sawdust is narrow, and it moves depending on how thick the piece is and whether it still has a bone. So this chart gives ranges you can start from. The number that decides whether dinner is safe is not on this page at all — it is the one your thermometer reads. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. Wattage and basket size change the clock, but 165°F / 74°C does not change. Why time alone is unreliable for chicken A 6-ounce breast and an 8-ounce breast look almost identical in the basket. One finishes in 14 minutes and the other needs 20. Bone-in pieces cook slower near the bone. A crowded basket slows everything down because the air cannot circulate. An air fryer also browns the outside long before the inside is done. That is why a piece can look perfect, smell perfect and still be undercooked in the center. Color, juices and firmness are all guesses. A thermometer is a measurement. x: Wings are the food the air fryer was practically made for: circulating hot air crisps the skin all over, with far less oil than deep frying and no oven splatter. The catch is that wings carry a lot of skin and fat, so they can look glossy and done while the joint is still undercooked. This chart gives starting times for fresh and frozen wings, plus the timing that keeps sauce from burning. This is the chart I keep on the fridge. Use it as a starting point, then trust your own machine for the final minute. t: Air Fryer Corn on the Cob: Times for Husked, In-Husk and Frozen
d: Air fryer corn on the cob times for husked, in-husk and frozen corn, with butter and oil handling and a note on reheating leftover corn safely.
x: Corn on the cob is the easiest side an air fryer makes. There is no pot of boiling water, no big kettle to drain, and the kernels come out with browned, slightly chewy spots that boiled corn never gets. It is also the one food on this site with no internal temperature to hit. Corn is a vegetable, and vegetables have no USDA safe internal temperature. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and poultry. For corn, use the clock and your eyes, and remember that wattage and basket size change the time. There is no safe internal temperature for corn This matters because it is a common question. USDA publishes safe internal temperatures for meat, poultry, fish, eggs and reheated leftovers, not for vegetables. Corn has no target number, so anyone quoting one for the kernels is inventing it. What corn does have is a doneness you can see. The kernels turn bright yellow, some of them brown at the tips, and a kernel pressed with a fork gives slightly. If the kernels look pale and flat, they need more time. The exception is leftover corn. Once corn has been cooked and refrigerated, reheating it puts it under the standard for reheated food, which is 165°F / 74°C. t: Air Fryer Desserts Chart (Cookies, Cakes and More)
d: Air fryer desserts chart with times and temperatures for cookies, mug cakes, brownies, cinnamon rolls, donuts, baked apples, s'mores and churros.
x: Dessert is the hardest thing to cook in an air fryer, and it is not close. A savoury dish tells you when it is done with colour and a thermometer. A cookie tells you nothing until you bite it. The heating element sits inches from the food, the fan pushes dry air across the surface, and the basket is small. Cakes and cookies set on the outside while the middle is still batter. This is the category where a chart is a starting point and nothing more. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. For desserts the thermometer measures the air, not the food: there is no safe internal temperature for a cookie. Use a toothpick. The rule that matters more than any number on this page There is no safe internal temperature for dessert. USDA internal-temperature guidance covers meat, poultry, eggs and leftovers, not cake batter, so anyone quoting you "the internal temperature of a brownie" is inventing a number. That leaves you two checks that actually work: Start checking early. If the chart says 15–18 min, look at 12 min. The last three minutes are where desserts go from underdone to ruined. Use the toothpick test. Insert a wooden toothpick or skewer into the centre and pull it out. A few moist crumbs are done. Wet batter is not. d: Air fryer hamburger times for fresh and frozen patties, with 380°F / 193°C settings, flip timing and the 160°F / 71°C ground beef rule.
x: The air fryer cooks burgers with the same hot air that crisps fries, so the outside browns and the fat that renders stays with the patty instead of dripping onto coals. It is faster than a grill to heat up and less messy than a skillet — but ground beef has a fixed safety rule, and a burger is the one shape where undercooking is easy to miss. The chart below covers fresh and frozen patties. Under USDA rules, ground beef must reach 160°F / 71°C inside — there is no thickness, cheese or bun that changes that number. t: Air Fryer Hard Boiled Eggs (Times by Doneness)
d: Air fryer hard boiled eggs by doneness, with soft, jammy and hard times, hot start and cold start methods, the ice bath and honest peeling notes.
x: Air frying eggs is not frying, and it is not boiling. You set whole eggs in the shell in the basket, run the machine low, and take them out with no pot to scrub. The results are real, and so are the limits. Here are the times by doneness, plus an honest answer on peeling. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and a timer for eggs. Wattage and basket size move the clock more for eggs than for anything else. Why people cook eggs in an air fryer Two reasons: hands-off cooking with no pot of water to heat, and the claim that air fryer eggs peel more easily, which this page deals with below. The trade is that a shell hides everything: you cannot see the yolk set, and you cannot read the center of an intact egg without breaking it. Time is your only control. d: Air fryer meal prep that actually holds up: what batches well, what turns to mush, the order to cook in, and the cooling and reheating rules.
x: An air fryer is a small, fast convection oven, which makes it a surprisingly good batch-cooking tool. It is also a small basket, so "batch" means several rounds, not one heroic load. The trick is planning the order. Cook in the wrong sequence and something sits raw on the counter while the machine is busy. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food. Treat every time below as a range, and verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. Start with the two rules Rule one: pull food by temperature, not by the clock. Two air fryers of the same size can differ by several minutes on the same potato. Rule two: everything waiting its turn goes in the refrigerator. Not on the counter, not on the stovetop. Food that sits out while you cook the next batch is the main way meal prep goes wrong. What batches well, and what does not This is the table that saves the most time. Some foods reheat better than they cook the first time; others should never be prepped in advance. d: Air fryer meatball times for beef, pork, turkey and chicken, fresh or frozen, with the 160°F / 71°C ground meat rule and no medium-rare.
x: Meatballs are one of the best things an air fryer does: they brown on every side without a pan of oil, they hold their shape if you handle them once, and they freeze and reheat well. They are also the clearest example of a rule people get wrong: a meatball is ground meat, and ground meat has no medium-rare. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer. The rule: ground meat has no medium-rare A whole steak can be served pink because the bacteria sit on the surface, where heat reaches them first. Grinding mixes that surface through the entire ball. Every part of the meatball is now surface, so the center has to reach the safe temperature. There is no pink middle that is safe by the same standard as a medium-rare steak. t: Air Fryer Mozzarella Sticks: Fresh and Frozen Times
d: Air fryer mozzarella stick times for frozen and homemade sticks, with the temperature that melts without bursting and the freeze-first rule.
x: Mozzarella sticks are the snack the air fryer handles better than any deep fryer: less oil, no splatter, and a crisp coating around a molten center. They are also the easiest snack to ruin — two extra minutes and the cheese bursts out of the coating and welds itself to the basket. This chart covers frozen and homemade sticks, plus the temperature logic that keeps the cheese inside where it belongs. Times vary by appliance model. t: Air Fryer Potatoes (Times and Temperatures by Cut)
d: Air fryer potatoes by cut: wedges, cubes, baby potatoes, slices, hash browns and sweet potatoes, with temperatures, times and the soak-and-dry rule.
x: Potatoes are the highest-volume air fryer question there is. The difference between a crisp wedge and a pale, limp one is not the machine — it is starch, water and space in the basket. Times vary by appliance model — use a thermometer for meat and your eyes for potatoes. Wattage, basket size and how full the basket is will move every number below. The starch rule: soak, then dry completely Cut potatoes release starch, and that starch is glue. It makes pieces stick together, steams the surfaces that touch, and leaves clumps that are crisp on one side and soft on the other. A 10–30 minute soak in cold water rinses that surface starch off. Drying matters more. Water on the surface has to evaporate before the potato can brown, so a wet potato steams first and crisps late. Drain, spread the pieces on a towel, and pat them dry. How much oil About 1 tablespoon of oil per pound of potatoes — roughly 15 mL per 450 g — and no more than 2 tablespoons for a full 2-pound basket. Toss until every piece has a faint sheen. More oil does not make crispier potatoes, just greasier ones, and the excess pools in the basket where it burns and smokes. Use a neutral oil with a high smoke point, and finish with butter or olive oil after the basket comes out. The energy goes into the water inside the food, and the surface never gets hot and dry enough to brown. x: Shrimp is the fastest protein an air fryer cooks. It is also the least forgiving. A three-minute mistake turns sweet and springy into rubber, and no sauce fixes that. Most of it is less than half an inch from the surface, so heat reaches the center almost as fast as it reaches the outside. There is no thick core to buy you time, which is why the useful window is about 30 to 60 seconds. The second reason is water. Shrimp are roughly three-quarters water, and as they heat that water squeezes out and the muscle fibers tighten. Past the safe temperature they keep tightening, and the texture turns firm, then chalky, then rubbery. Shrimp also carry enzymes that turn them mushy if they sit at a lukewarm temperature too long. Shrimp are sold by count per pound, and the label is the size. U/15 means under 15 shrimp per pound, which is jumbo. 31/40 means 31 to 40 per pound, which is small. d: What each air fryer temperature is for, from 320°F / 160°C for delicate foods to 400°F / 205°C for crisping, with adjustments for frozen food.
x: Most air fryer confusion is temperature confusion. The machine can hold anything from 180°F / 82°C to 400°F / 205°C, and the difference between perfect and disappointing is usually just picking the right rung on that ladder — then leaving the food alone long enough. This guide maps the common settings to the jobs they do best, explains why frozen food and fresh food rarely use the same number, and covers the adjustments that recipes assume you already know. Times vary by appliance model. Wattage changes how fast a setting reaches the food, so use times as starting points and verify doneness the usual way. What the air fryer actually does with temperature An air fryer is a compact convection oven: a heating element and a fan that pushes hot air around a small space. Because the chamber is small, the air moves fast and transfers heat more aggressively than a conventional oven at the same dial setting. That is why air fryer temperatures run 25°F / 14°C to 50°F / 28°C lower than the oven temperatures printed on frozen food bags. The practical rule: when converting an oven recipe, subtract 25°F / 14°C and check for doneness about 20 percent earlier. An air fryer is easy to clean if you do it often. The two mistakes people make — soaking the whole appliance and scrubbing with abrasive pads — are exactly the ones that cause damage. Cleaning guidance varies by appliance model — read your manual before you soak, scrub or dishwasher anything. t: Oven to Air Fryer Conversion Chart (Temperatures and Times)
d: Convert any oven recipe to an air fryer: lower the temperature about 25°F / 15°C, cut the time about 20 percent, and know when conversion fails.
x: An air fryer is a small convection oven with the element inches from the food. That proximity is why an oven recipe overcooks in it: same food, same temperature, much more heat where it counts. The fix is three adjustments. They are rules of thumb, not a formula. Air fryer models differ in wattage, basket size and how close the element sits to the food. Treat every time below as a range, and verify doneness with an instant-read thermometer. The three general rules Rule one: lower the temperature by roughly 25°F / 15°C. Air fryer dials are usually calibrated at the element, not at the food, and the food sits much closer to it. Rule two: cut the time by roughly 20 percent. A 25–30 min oven step becomes about 20–24 min. Rule three: check early. Open the basket at about two-thirds of the converted time. Once something is over-browned, there is no way back. Two constraints matter as much as the numbers. The basket holds one layer, so a sheet-pan recipe becomes two or three rounds. And most air fryers need a 3–5 min preheat for browning.
